newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Australia wheat said not undermining market.
newsitem.headline: Australia wheat said not undermining market.

text.p: Recent Australian wheat sales to India, Iran and Sudan reflect strong import demand and have not undercut the market, an Australian trade official said.
"There's steady demand. The sales are not coming with lower prices," said the official.
The official added that Australian white wheat commanded a substantial premium over EU wheat due to its higher breadmaking quality.

But EU traders and member state grain officials have been urging the European Commission to use export subsidies more aggressively to help farmers compete with Australia as it disposes of a record 23-million-tonne crop.
Although with its August harvest it has a four-month start over Australia, the EU still has some four million tonnes of unsold 1996/97 wheat worth half a billion dollars.
Australia is concerned that the European Commission may renege on a pledge to Washington, its traditional rival for wheat markets, and step up the use of export subsidies.
"We are worried that the EU may start increasing export refunds," the official said.
Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson will raise the issue when he meets Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler in Canberra in early February.
The Australian Wheat Board said earlier this month it expects to export 17 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97, almost 50 percent more than for a normal crop.
Much of the crop will have to be exported in the second half of the marketing season.
"There will be some overlap (with the EU new crop) this time round," said the Australian official in Brussels. "It's a new development."
The same applies for other Northern hemisphere producers.

But an EU grain trade source in Brussels played down speculation of a wheat war with Australia, noting that Argentina was a bigger threat because its lack of starge capacity forced it to offload its harvest as quickly as possible.
EU 1996/97 soft wheat exports are much higher than last year and French shipments have been boosted by Iraq's return to the market, he noted.
But Britain could have problems, especially as its wheat would have difficulty meeting intervention quality standards, as well as Germany which has large on-farm stocks.
